extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, especially fathers/householders and members of the nobility (early-modern France) interested in moral conduct and domestic governance
extracted.subtask_description: Montaigne's prescriptive essays on the proper handling of public honours and the domestic duties of fathers: how honours should be conferred and why, and how parents should educate, support, and comport themselves toward their children as they age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour derives its value from rarity
rubrics_metrics.description: “honour is a privilege which derives its principal essence from rarity; and so virtue itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honours and distinctions are valuable because few possess them; proliferating them or making them common destroys their value. The essay argues that honours should be granted sparingly to preserve dignity and estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix material gain with honours
rubrics_metrics.description: “If with the reward, which ought to be simply a recompense of honour, they should mix other commodities and add riches, this mixture, instead of procuring an increase of estimation, would debase and abate it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary or profitable attachments to honours corrupt their symbolic worth; honours are best as non‑material, ceremonial recognitions separate from financial rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic, non‑costly distinctions to reward merit
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a very good and profitable custom to find out an acknowledgment for the worth of rare and excellent men, and to satisfy them with rewards that are not at all chargeable either to prince or people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instituting valueless (symbolic) distinctions—crowns of laurel, titles, privileges of place—can acknowledge merit without fiscal burden and without the corrupting effects of money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer high command/strategic merit for premier orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The recompense of this order had not only a regard to valour, but had a further prospect; it never was the reward of a valiant soldier but of a great captain; the science of obeying was not reputed worthy of so honourable a guerdon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top honours ought to recognize wider military (or civic) excellence and leadership, not only individual acts of courage or routine service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and honour lose distinction when they become customary
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no recompense becomes virtue, how great soever, that is once passed into a custom; and I know not withal whether we can ever call it great, being common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a virtue or honour becomes ordinary practice across a community, it ceases to be praiseworthy in the same way—rarity underpins esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not liberalize honours merely because more are 'deserving'
rubrics_metrics.description: Though there should be now more men found than in former times worthy of our order, the estimation of it nevertheless should not be abated, nor the honour made cheap; and it may easily happen that more may merit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if more people appear to deserve an honour, broadening distribution risks devaluing it; better to err on the side of restraint than to cheapen the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental affection should be guided by reason and grow with the child
rubrics_metrics.description: A true and regular affection ought to spring and increase with the knowledge they give us of themselves, and then, if they are worthy of it, the natural propension walking hand in hand with reason, to cherish them with a truly paternal love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affection for children should not be merely instinctive indulgence toward infants but should develop as the child demonstrates character and worth; judgement should moderate natural inclinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive fondling of infants; love should follow discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot entertain that passion of dandling and caressing infants scarcely born... I have not willingly suffered them to be nursed near me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes excessive, early pampering (dandling) that attaches affection to mere infantile playfulness rather than to the child's developing virtues or reasoned merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fathers should share goods and include children in their patrimony
rubrics_metrics.description: I think it cruelty and injustice not to receive them into the share and society of our goods, and not to make them partakers in the intelligence of our domestic affairs when they are capable, and not to lessen and contract our own expenses to make the more room for theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unjust for old parents to hoard wealth to the detriment of their children; parents should provide for children's advancement (education, position) rather than preserving wealth solely for their own comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoarding by parents can drive children to vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A man by this course drives them to despair, and to seek out by any means, how unjust or dishonourable soever, to provide for their own support... I have seen several young men of good extraction so addicted to stealing... put upon this paltry practice by the severity and avarice of his father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental stinginess not only breaches justice but has practical harms (poverty leading to theft or dishonourable acts); generosity and appropriate provisioning prevent such outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should rely on reason, prudence, and gentle correction, not violence
rubrics_metrics.description: I condemn all violence in the education of a tender soul that is designed for honour and liberty... what is not to be done by reason, prudence, and address, is never to be affected by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reports minimal corporal punishment in his upbringing and recommends gentle, reasoned instruction over harsh correction, arguing that force breeds servility or obstinacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not marry too young; prefer mature ages for marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: I married at three-and-thirty years of age, and concur in the opinion of thirty-five, which is said to be that of Aristotle. Plato will have nobody marry before thirty...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marriage should be delayed until maturity (he cites 30–35) so parents are not too close in age to their children and so fathers can better govern and provide for their household.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aged parents should cede use of possessions when they become burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: The remaining pomps, of which he has no further use, he ought voluntarily to surrender to those, to whom by the order of nature they belong... he resigned his possessions, grandeur, and power to his son, when he found himself failing in vigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When age renders goods and offices unfit for one's use, it is reasonable and honorable to transfer enjoyment and administration to the next generation while possibly keeping a revocable oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain familiarity and affection; forbidding 'father' is foolish
rubrics_metrics.description: I am angry at the custom of forbidding children to call their father by the name of father... We call Almighty God Father, and disdain to have our children call us so; I have reformed this error in my family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid, courtly forms of address that prevent familial closeness are misguided; natural familiarity helps secure love and respect more effectively than austere forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer being loved by your family rather than feared
rubrics_metrics.description: Though I could make myself feared, I had yet much rather make myself beloved: there are so many sorts of defects in old age... that the best acquisition a man can make is the kindness and affection of his own family; command and fear are no longer his weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In old age, authority via fear is ineffective and humiliating; cultivating affection and friendship with one’s children yields better dignity and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid solitary retirement and excessive seclusion in old age
rubrics_metrics.description: He had been given up to such a solitude... he would, hardly once in a week, suffer any one to come in to see him... I would endeavour by pleasant conversation to create in my children a warm and unfeigned friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes extreme seclusion (examples of clergy who never left their rooms) and recommends staying engaged with family in a measured way—living near them, conversing, instructing—rather than cutting oneself off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of domestic deceit; cultivate trustworthy friendship and self‑awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: So many servants, so many enemies... I exalt the value of a friend, in comparison with these civil ties... I protect myself from such treasons in my own bosom, not by an unquiet and tumultuous curiosity, but rather by diversion and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household ties (servants, spouse, children) can become sources of exploitation in old age; Montaigne urges prudence, self-examination, and valuing genuine friends as safeguards against domestic treacheries.
